issues.legal_issue: The admissibility of an instrument is determined by its recitals, not by an opposing party’s pleadings about whether the recited event occurred.
material_facts: The agreement on which the suit was founded stated that the seller had handed over physical possession to the purchaser.
The defendants denied both executing the agreement and delivering possession, while the plaintiffs sought possession as part of their relief.
The trial court was considering whether to admit the agreement in evidence.
issues.conclusion: For deciding admissibility, the terms and recitals of the instrument govern, notwithstanding the defendants’ denial of possession; whether possession was actually delivered remains a question of fact for adjudication, and the recital is not conclusive on that question.
issues.legal_principle: The court determines admissibility from the instrument’s own terms rather than the parties’ pleadings. Whether possession was in fact delivered is a separate factual question. The court relied on the principle stated in Avinash Kumar Chauhan v. Vijay Krishna Mishra, (2009) 2 SCC 532, and agreed with the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s later conclusion in Man Singh (deceased) through Legal Representatives v. Rameshwar.

predicates.evidence_admissibility_review: A court is deciding whether an instrument may be received in evidence.
predicates.instrument_recites_transfer_of_possessio: The instrument states that one party handed possession of property to another party.

issues.definition: When a court reviews an instrument’s admissibility and the instrument recites a transfer of possession, the recital controls the admissibility assessment.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement for the sale of immovable property that records transfer of possession is treated as a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes and, if insufficiently stamped, is inadmissible until the required duty and penalty are paid.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property and recorded payment of part of the consideration and delivery of physical possession to the purchaser.

The applicable Madhya Pradesh stamp-law amendment treated an agreement to sell immovable property as a conveyance where possession was transferred before or after the agreement without execution of a conveyance.
The agreement bore only a nominal stamp, which was insufficient for the duty chargeable as on a conveyance.
The question arose while the trial court was deciding whether to admit the agreement in evidence.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes and was insufficiently stamped; the trial court rightly refused to admit it, subject to the statutory procedure for admission upon payment of the deficient duty and penalty.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(10) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 defines conveyance to include an instrument transferring property inter vivos. Section 3 makes chargeable instruments liable to duty, and the Explanation to Article 23 of Schedule 1-A, as substituted by the Madhya Pradesh Indian Stamp (Madhya Pradesh Second Amendment) Act, 1990, deems an agreement to sell immovable property to be a conveyance where possession is transferred without a conveyance being executed. Section 35 bars admission of an instrument that is not duly stamped, while permitting admission on payment of the required duty or deficient portion and penalty. The court relied on Avinash Kumar Chauhan v. Vijay Krishna Mishra, (2009) 2 SCC 532.

issues.definition: If an evidence-admissibility review concerns an immovable-property sale agreement that recites transfer of possession, the applicable stamp framework covers that kind of agreement, and the full duty has not been paid, the agreement remains inadmissible until the duty and penalty are paid.
